paras: The attempted lynching of Riley Park took place at Clarendon, Arkansas, on the night of May 22, 1903, when about twenty-five men came into town intending to lynch Park, a Black man accused of shooting a white farmer named Fowler. Sheriff Milwee had already sent Park away to Little Rock, and the mob went home without violence. The case drew notice again a month later, when a Clarendon dispatch cited the mob's failure to reach Park as a reason for the lynching of Jack Harris in the same neighborhood.

The shooting grew out of a dispute over Park's livestock, which, according to a special dispatch to the St. Louis Republic, had broken into Fowler's field. The day before, Fowler had Park arraigned in a justice court, and when Park admitted sending "certain insulting messages," Fowler attacked him in the courtroom and, the dispatch said, would have killed him had officers not intervened. On the morning of Wednesday, May 20, about ten miles east of Clarendon, Park shot Fowler, who was reported "probably fatally wounded." The Republic's correspondent wrote that Fowler had gone to Park's house "with the avowed purpose of killing him" and that Park "got the first shot." Park then went to Clarendon and surrendered to Sheriff Milwee.

Suspecting that a lynching would be attempted, Milwee had Park taken out of Clarendon early on the evening of May 22, sending him by buggy to Brinkley and from there to Little Rock, where he was to stay until the fall term of the circuit court. Later that night about twenty-five men from what the dispatch called "the Park neighborhood" came into town "bent on lynching" him. Finding Park gone, the men, whom the dispatch described as "orderly," returned to their homes.

Later items said Fowler had died: a June 4 news column in the Monticellonian said Park had "shot and killed John Fowler, a prominent white citizen, near Holly Grove," and a June 25 Clarendon dispatch called Park the man "who killed a white man named Fowler." Both items said Park had been placed in the penitentiary at Little Rock, the second saying Milwee was "forced" to send him there for safekeeping. No report of an inquest into Fowler's death, or of an indictment or trial of Park, was found in the coverage.

The June 25 dispatch, reporting the lynching of Jack Harris, whom it said had seriously injured a white man named John Coburn, argued that such "severe measures" might not have been taken had the mob not failed with Park. It added that since Park's removal Black residents of the Coburn neighborhood were "said to have grown very insolent," while noting that the Harris lynching was "deplored by many citizens."

The episode appears only in the white press; no Black-press report of it was found. The first report, a special dispatch to the St. Louis Republic headed "Negro Shoots White Man," framed the shooting by race but included details that cast Fowler as the aggressor, his courtroom attack and his armed visit to Park's house. A two-sentence version that left out those details ran as a state news brief in the Monticellonian on May 28 and in the Van Buren Press on May 30.

The mob itself appeared in a single Clarendon dispatch in the Newport Daily Independent of May 25, headlined "Sheriff Outwitted Mob," which credited the sheriff's foresight and called the mob "orderly" without criticizing it. The Monticellonian's June brief, which turned the shooting into a killing, said Park had "escaped death at the hands of a mob." By late June the Newport paper treated the failed attempt as an explanation for the next lynching at Clarendon rather than as news in itself.

The May reports gave Fowler's name as "J. O." or "Jo" Fowler and called him probably fatally wounded, while the June items named him John Fowler and said he had been killed, a difference that may reflect his death after the first reports. The Republic's dated Clarendon dispatch placed the shooting ten miles east of town, whereas the Monticellonian's later, unsourced brief put it near Holly Grove.

reader.title: Attempted lynching of Riley Park
bases: A mob of about twenty-five men came to Clarendon 'bent on lynching' Park, a Black man in the sheriff's custody, and left when they found he had been removed (A2, A5); the lynching was threatened, not carried out.

About twenty-five men sought to lynch Park in revenge for his shooting of Fowler, an extralegal purpose by a group of three or more (A2, A6), but the sheriff had removed him and no one was killed (A2, A5).

The mob's visit is told in one Clarendon dispatch (A2), but two later items with details A2 lacks independently report that Park escaped a mob after the sheriff spirited him away (A5, A6); the shooting itself is reported by A1 and A3.

Headlined 'Sheriff Outwitted Mob', credited the sheriff's foresight and called the mob 'orderly' without criticism.
Arkansas weeklies ran short state-news briefs, the later one upgrading the shooting to a killing of 'a prominent white citizen'.

The June Newport dispatch presented the failed attempt on Park as a reason for the Harris lynching and repeated that Black residents had 'grown very insolent', while noting the lynching was 'deplored by many citizens'.
